title: Design a Proximity Service (Yelp / 'Nearby' / Uber)
tagline: Find what's near me, fast — the geospatial indexing problem behind maps, ride-hailing, and local search.
summary: Geohashing, quadtrees, spatial indexing, read-heavy search.

blocks.title: Functional
items: Given a user's location (lat, lng) and a radius, return businesses/objects within it.
Add / update / delete places (or moving objects like drivers).
Return details for a selected place.

blocks.title: Non-functional
items: Low latency on search — users expect instant results.
Read-heavy for static places (Yelp); write-heavy for moving objects (Uber driver locations).
Scalable to hundreds of millions of places and high query volume.

blocks.text: The core challenge is spatial: a standard B-tree index can't efficiently answer 'within X km of (lat,lng)' because 2D proximity isn't a 1D range. The whole design hinges on a geospatial index that turns 2D space into something searchable.

paragraphs: Naively: `SELECT * FROM places WHERE distance(lat,lng, ?, ?) < radius`. This computes distance to *every* row — a full table scan over hundreds of millions of places per query. Even indexing latitude and longitude separately doesn't help much: an index on latitude returns a thin horizontal band of the whole planet, an index on longitude a thin vertical band, and intersecting them is expensive. We need an index built for 2D proximity.

blocks.text: The trap is proposing two separate B-tree indexes on lat and lng. Interviewers want you to recognize that 2D nearest-neighbor needs a spatial structure (geohash / quadtree / R-tree / S2), not two 1D indexes.

paragraphs: Geohashing recursively divides the world map into a grid and encodes each cell as a short string. Each added character refines the cell to a smaller area. The key property: **places that are physically close usually share a geohash prefix.**

items.detail: Longer shared prefix → closer together. A 6-char geohash is roughly a ~1.2 km cell; 5-char ~5 km. Pick precision to match the search radius.

Because a geohash is just a string, you can store it in a normal database/cache and do a prefix query (or exact-cell lookup) — which a standard index handles efficiently. This is the magic: 2D proximity becomes a 1D string-prefix problem.
Compute the user's geohash at the right precision, fetch places in that cell, and — to handle objects near a cell boundary — also fetch the 8 neighboring cells, then rank by exact distance.

blocks.title: The boundary problem
blocks.text: Two points can be meters apart but fall in different cells (and thus share no/short prefix) if they straddle a boundary. Always query the surrounding 8 neighbor cells too, then filter by true distance. This is the classic gotcha to mention.

paragraphs: A quadtree is an in-memory tree that recursively subdivides space into four quadrants, but only where density is high. Dense areas (downtown SF) split into many small cells; sparse areas (desert) stay as one big cell.

blocks.title: Geohash vs Quadtree
rows: Fixed grid — dense cells get huge, sparse cells empty
Adaptive — splits only where dense (balanced cell sizes)
Just strings in a DB/cache — easy to persist & shard
In-memory tree — must rebuild on startup / from DB
More complex, but elegant for skewed density
Rebalancing the tree on heavy churn is costlier

blocks.text: Both are valid; mention the trade-off. Geohash is simpler to store and shard (great default). Quadtrees adapt to skewed density. Production systems often use Google S2 (a sophisticated geohash-like cell library) or PostGIS / database geospatial indexes (R-trees).

blocks.caption: A read-optimized location service backed by a geo-indexed store and cache.

items.detail: Places rarely move → extremely read-heavy. Precompute geohashes, store `geohash → list of place IDs`, and cache aggressively. Replicas + cache absorb the query load.

Drivers send location updates every few seconds → write-heavy. Don't persist every ping to disk; keep current locations in an in-memory geo-index (e.g., Redis with geo commands) updated continuously, and only periodically checkpoint. The grid cell a driver belongs to changes as they move.
Shard by geohash prefix (region) so a query usually hits one shard. Beware hot regions (a concert, downtown rush hour) — use finer cells or replicate hot shards.

blocks.text: The senior insight is recognizing the two regimes: static-and-read-heavy (cache geohash buckets) vs moving-and-write-heavy (in-memory grid, frequent updates, periodic checkpointing). Tailor storage to which one you're asked about, and call out hot-cell load as the scaling risk.

cheatsheet: 2D nearest-neighbor needs a spatial index — two separate B-tree indexes on lat/lng don't work.
Geohash: recursively grid the map into prefix-coded cells; close points share a prefix → 2D proximity becomes 1D prefix search.
Always query the 8 neighbor cells too (boundary problem), then rank by true distance.
Quadtree: adaptive subdivision — splits only dense regions; in-memory, more complex but handles skew.
Production: Google S2, PostGIS/R-trees, or Redis geo commands.
Static places (Yelp) = read-heavy → precompute geohashes + cache; moving objects (Uber) = write-heavy → in-memory grid + periodic checkpoint.
Shard by geohash/region; watch for hot cells (downtown, events) and split/replicate them.

questions.prompt: Why can't you just index latitude and longitude columns separately, and how does geohashing solve it?
questions.hint: Think about what a 1D index returns for a 2D proximity query.
answer: A B-tree index on latitude lets you fetch a thin horizontal band of the entire planet (all places within some latitude range); an index on longitude gives a thin vertical band. To find places near a point you'd intersect these two enormous bands and then distance-filter — the intersection is huge and the work scales with how many places fall in those global strips, not with how many are actually nearby. 1D indexes don't capture 2D locality.

Geohashing fixes this by mapping 2D coordinates to a single string such that physical proximity becomes shared-prefix proximity. You recursively divide the map into a grid; each cell gets a code, and longer codes mean smaller cells. Because nearby points share a long prefix, finding neighbors is a prefix lookup (or exact-cell lookup) on a single ordinary string index — efficient and shardable. You compute the user's geohash at a precision matching the radius, pull that cell plus its 8 neighbors (to handle boundary cases), and rank the candidates by exact distance. The query now scales with the local density, not the global table size.
keyPoints: 1D index on lat/lng returns global bands; intersection is expensive and not local
Geohash maps 2D → 1D string where proximity = shared prefix
Prefix/exact-cell lookup on a normal index is efficient & shardable
Query the cell + 8 neighbors, then rank by true distance
followUps: How do you choose the geohash precision for a given search radius?

questions.prompt: For Uber, drivers send location updates every 4 seconds. How does the design differ from a static Yelp-style service?
questions.hint: Write-heavy + ephemeral data vs read-heavy + durable data.
answer: Yelp places are essentially static and the workload is read-heavy, so you precompute each place's geohash, store `geohash → place IDs`, and cache the buckets aggressively; reads are served from cache/replicas and writes are rare. Uber inverts this: with millions of drivers pinging every ~4 seconds, it's write-heavy, and the data is ephemeral (only the *current* location matters, not the history of every ping).

So you don't durably persist every update to a disk-based DB — that's a write storm with no value. Instead keep current driver locations in an in-memory geospatial index (e.g., Redis geo, or an in-memory quadtree/grid) keyed by cell, updating in place as drivers move between cells. You only periodically checkpoint to durable storage for crash recovery. Reads ('drivers near this rider') query the rider's cell + neighbors from the in-memory index. The scaling risks shift too: hot cells during rush hour or near an event get a flood of both updates and queries, so you shard by region and split/replicate hot cells, and you may relax precision under load. In short: ephemeral, in-memory, write-optimized, checkpointed — versus Yelp's durable, cache-optimized, read-heavy design.
keyPoints: Uber = write-heavy + ephemeral (only current location matters)
Keep live locations in-memory (Redis geo / in-memory grid), update in place
Don't persist every ping — periodic checkpoint for recovery only
Hot cells (events/rush hour) are the scaling risk → shard/split/replicate by region
followUps: How would you match a rider to the nearest available driver while many riders search the same hot cell simultaneously?
